title: Math Gaps Don't Start in College
author: Aldeman, Chad
summary: Drawing on a new report he authored with the Collaborative for Student Success on math preparedness at Rutgers, the author argues that college math gaps are not created in the transition from senior year of high school to college; they build up over years of the K-12 system passing students along despite falling behind. He points to New Jersey's newly released state test data showing proficiency rates falling from 47.9% in 3rd grade to 37.4% by 7th grade, a 'waterfall pattern' also seen in other states, as evidence that math skill gaps compound cumulatively rather than resolve on their own. With roughly 60% of New Jersey students unable to pass the state's Algebra I exam, the piece argues that by the time affected students reach a college campus like Rutgers, the problem is far more expensive and difficult to fix than if it had been addressed years earlier. The core argument is a call to intervene at the K-12 level, where math gaps first appear, rather than treating college remediation as the primary fix point.
points: Read state math scores top-to-bottom by grade, not just year-over-year, to see the 'waterfall' pattern of proficiency declining as students move through elementary and middle school.
Recognize that math is cumulative, so gaps that open in elementary school compound rather than self-correct as students advance.
Intervene on math preparation in K-12, years before students reach college remediation, rather than waiting for placement tests at the university level.
Treat college math-remediation reports as downstream evidence of upstream K-12 instructional gaps, not a college-readiness problem in isolation.
quotes: students didn’t just lose their math skills between the spring of their senior year of high school and when they show up on the Rutgers campus in the fall. More likely, many of them had been falling behind for years, while the K-12 system continued passing them along.
This year, 47.9% of New Jersey’s 3rd graders reached the state’s proficiency target in math... For 7th graders, just 37.4% of students reached the state standard.
Math is a cumulative subject, and students don’t just naturally recover and improve over time. Instead, more and more students fall off track with each passing year.
it’s not a great sign that 60% of New Jersey students couldn’t pass the state’s Algebra I exam…
By the time those students arrive on a college campus, the problem will be much harder and more expensive to fix.
the better time to intervene was years earlier, when the gaps first appeared.
